units: the heart races and the hands sweat before speaking in front of a group
the person going through it believes she is fragile and judges herself clumsy
the fear pushes her to avoid meetings where she would have to speak
avoidance strengthens the fear instead of reducing it
breathing out more slowly than you breathe in slows the heartbeat
rehearsing the opening line aloud at home helps with getting started
it is better to put up with the early trembling than to fight it
a relaxed friend can serve as a practice audience
the panic wears down after several repeated attempts
text: You know the feeling. Your heart takes off, your palms go damp, and your throat locks shut right before the first word to a room full of people. Anyone who goes through it decides she is fragile, that she comes across as clumsy, and soon she is ducking every meeting where somebody might call on her. That is where the trap shuts. Dodge the room and the fear grows instead of shrinking. What gets you out is dull and practical. Breathe from the belly, letting the air out more slowly than you drew it in, and the heartbeat settles on its own. Say your opening line aloud at home until your mouth already knows the road. Let the early trembling happen rather than wrestling it down. A friend who is easy company makes a fine practice audience. After enough tries, the panic simply wears out.

units: two opposite positions go around about the place of feelings in a team
the first one demands complete restraint and admits nothing but arguments
the second one prizes the open expression of anger and grief
imposed silence sends the unease around underground
compulsory restraint leaves colleagues quicker to take offence
expression without limits wears out the people listening
a middle way is to name your own state without demanding that it be repaired
this balance sounds obvious to state but has to be learned
text: Raise the place of feelings in a team and two camps start shouting past each other. The first wants them held back altogether: the steady professional parks his moods at the door and brings nothing to the table but arguments. The second cheers for saying it plainly, anger out loud, grief owned in front of colleagues. Each camp is right about its rival and wrong about itself. Enforced silence does not clear the unease away, it drives it underground, where it spreads and where the mildest remark leaves everyone quick to take offence. Pouring it out without limit wears the listeners down until no one is listening at all. What holds is narrower than either: name what you feel without asking anyone to repair it. Saying you are worn thin obliges no colleague to console you. Easy to state, slow to learn.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the listener works evenings with a headset on a helpline
the people who call stay anonymous
her voice stays low and never rises
her first quality is putting up with long silences
her second quality is holding on to details given early in the call
her third quality is a welcoming tone that promises nothing
one caller who said little took an hour before producing a whole sentence
she will never know what became of the people she listened to
text: The voice comes first, low and level, and it never climbs, not even when the line is jammed. She spends her evenings at a helpline with a headset on, taking calls from strangers in pieces who give no name at any point. Three gifts hold the work together. Patience is the first: she lets silences run on where anyone else would hurry to fill them. Memory for small things is the second; a dog mentioned in the opening minute comes back out of her mouth much later. The third is warmth without false closeness, a tone that steadies while promising nothing at all. She tells of one guarded caller who took a whole hour before a full sentence arrived. What became of him she will never learn. That is the heaviest part of the work: shelter for a single evening, and then the line goes dead.

units: the program under review is made of four successive stages
the opening session serves to list what sets the anxiety off
the self-rating scale stays understandable with no training behind it
the breathing work locks every participant to one and the same pace
that single pace ignores the differences in lung capacity
graded exposure is the best designed part of the program
the ladder of feared situations is built together with the patient
the last session handles relapse prevention on a single sheet
the final judgement is mixed: rigorous middle, rigid opening, rushed ending
text: The program under review runs through four stages, and each earns a verdict of its own. It opens with a structured interview in which the practitioner lists whatever sets the anxiety off. That part is sound: the questions stay open, and the self-rating scale reads clearly to someone with no training behind him. The breathing work that follows is harder to defend, since the instruction locks every participant to one pace while lung capacity plainly differs from person to person. Stage three, graded exposure, is where the design holds best: the ladder of feared situations gets built with the patient rather than handed to him. The closing session then disposes of relapse prevention on one photocopied sheet. The judgement comes out mixed, rigorous through the middle, rigid at the door and rushed at the exit.

units: the writer is explaining a long absence he has never justified clearly
the death of his sister happened a short while ago
the grief did not fade the way he had assumed it would
the writer turned inattentive and let files slip his mind
he would read the same page over without holding on to any of it
this scattering damaged the quality of his reports
out of that grew a sense of being no longer capable
that sense led him to turn down the invitations of his team
his silence was taken for contempt
he is starting treatment and wants to come back in stages
text: I am writing to you about my long absence, which I have never explained with any clarity. My sister died a short while ago, and the effect on me was not the one I had assumed. I expected the grief to settle in and then thin out; it took quite another road. First it left me inattentive. Files slipped my mind, and I would read the same page over and over without holding on to a line of it. My reports suffered for that scattering, and out of the poor work grew a conviction that I was no longer capable. From the conviction came avoidance: I stopped answering the invitations of my team, and the silence was read as contempt. I can see how opaque that chain must have looked from where you sit. I have begun treatment with a specialist, and I would like to resume my duties in stages.

units: the question raised is whether sleep can be learned when the mind will not settle
insomnia feeds itself through the dread of not sleeping
the long waking hours then prove that dread right
the first piece of advice is to cut down the time spent in bed
the window is then widened step by step once falling asleep turns quick again
leaving the bed when the night drags on is advised
this instruction keeps the bed from standing for a struggle
the effect of screens is real but it is overstated
a racing mind counts for more than screens do
text: One question keeps coming back in consultations: can a person learn to sleep when the mind refuses to switch off? The accepted answer opens on an unwelcome note. Insomnia feeds itself. Dread of a sleepless night keeps you awake, and the waking hours then prove the dread right. So what is to be done? The first piece of advice startles people, since it asks for less time in bed rather than more. You narrow the window until falling asleep turns quick again, then widen it step by step. A second question comes up often: get out of bed when the night drags on? Yes, say the protocols, so that the bed stops standing for a struggle. And screens? Their effect is real but overstated; a racing mind weighs heavier. One rule holds throughout: a restless head settles better upright than lying down.

units: the older brother tells his sister he cannot make sense of their mother
their mother flares up over a tiny mishap but stays calm at bad news
the sister describes their father as working the other way around
the father says nothing during a crisis and turns pleasant once things are quiet
the mother lets the anger out fast and forgets it fast
the father stores it up and then caves in weeks later
the brother finds the loud way more hurtful because the words land straight
the sister prefers that way because you know where you stand
both of them admit they were handed a model without choosing it
text: The older brother told his sister he had given up making sense of their mother. She would shout over a spilled glass, he said, and then take bad news without a flicker. His sister answered that their father ran the other way around: not a word out of him while things fell apart, then all charm once the house went quiet. One lets it out fast and comes down fast, she said, and forgets it within the hour. The other stores it, holds on to it, and caves in weeks later out of nowhere. The brother argued that the loud way cuts deeper, because the words land straight in your face. His sister thought the opposite: at least you know where you stand, while a long silence leaves you guessing at anything. Neither way was better, they agreed, and neither of them had picked the one they were handed.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: three readings of mental suffering came before the scientific discipline
these readings piled onto one another rather than replacing one another
the supernatural reading put the trouble down to a force from outside
it treated through ceremonies meant to drive that force back out
the reading by inner fluids explained melancholy by an imbalance of the body
it reached for bleedings, purges and strict diets
the moral reading held the sufferer answerable for his own disorder
it prescribed fixed hours, work with the hands and removal from other people
each reading brought forth its own institutions and its own words
phrases born of these readings live on in everyday speech
text: Long before the study of the mind turned into a discipline, mental suffering was read in three ways, and the later ones piled onto the earlier rather than clearing them off. The first reading was supernatural: something from outside had taken hold, so the cure lay in ceremonies meant to drive it back out. The second put the fault in the body, blaming melancholy on inner fluids gone out of balance; patients were bled, purged and held to strict diets. The third was moral. It held the sufferer answerable for his own disorder and bet on discipline, on fixed hours, work with the hands and removal from other people. Each reading raised its own houses, its own trades, its own words. Everyday speech carries them still, in talk of black moods and possessed minds. Careful clinical observation came last, and took generations to win.

units: the newborn has only three signals of feeling at his disposal
these signals are distress, calm and a wide awake curiosity
near the close of the first year comes fear of unfamiliar faces
that fear shows the child now sorts the close ones from the strangers
in front of a mirror the child works out at last that the smudge is on his own forehead
out of that recognition come embarrassment, pride and shame
school teaches that a feeling can be kept out of sight
the child discovers that a soothing face can lie
in adolescence the charge of feeling swells before the power to hold back does
that gap explains how hard the outbursts of that age break
text: Watch a newborn and the whole repertoire fits into three signals: distress, calm, and a wide awake sort of curiosity. Everything that follows grows out of there. Near the close of the first year comes unease at an unfamiliar face, proof that the child now sorts the close ones from the strangers. Then the self arrives. Put in front of a mirror, the child works out at last that the smudge belongs to his own forehead, and out of that recognition come embarrassment, pride and shame. School lays down a further layer: a feeling can be kept out of sight, a soothing face can lie, tears come less freely with an audience nearby. In adolescence the charge swells while the brake matures late, which is why the storms of those years break so hard. The finished structure takes decades to raise.

units: an incident on a hospital ward illustrates how a state of feeling spreads
the nurse in charge of the ward took bad family news as her shift began
she told no colleague about it
her speech quickened and her instructions came out clipped
the team changed its behaviour within two handovers
exchanges grew shorter and cross-checks fell away
the number of preparation errors doubled
the review afterwards ruled out fatigue and patient load as explanations
the cause settled on is the silent passing of a state through posture, gaze and pace of speech
a short debriefing meeting put the coordination back
text: An incident on a hospital ward gave a clean illustration of how a state of feeling spreads. The nurse in charge, unflappable as a rule, took bad news about her family just as her shift began. She said nothing about it to any colleague. Her speech quickened all the same, and her instructions came out clipped. Within two handovers the whole team had shifted: exchanges grew shorter, cross-checks fell away, and the mood on the floor turned heavy. The measurable consequence showed up in the incident log, where preparation errors doubled. The review afterwards ruled out fatigue and patient load, both of which had held steady. What was left was the silent passing of a state through posture, gaze and the pace of speech. A short debriefing meeting was enough to put the coordination back.
